doc.title: Nick Brignola interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 28, 1997

title: Playing along with the radio; Kenton, Thornhill and Paul Desmond
summary: He learned countless big band tunes off the radio, then was drawn to Kenton and Thornhill harmonies and to Paul Desmond.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Right. And also the material that he was training me to play was not what I wanted to play. So I used to play with the radio. I would listen — most of the — well you may not have been around them, but most of the band leaders back then played clarinet. It was Benny Goodman, Artie Shaw, Jimmy Dorsey, Woody Herman. Clarinet was all over the place. So I used to just play along with the radio. And most of the pop music of the day was the big band music. So that’s what I grew up on. I learned a million tunes — not really knowing that I was learning tunes. And then came the ‘50s. I heard Stan Kenton’s band. And that band stuck out because the harmonies in that band had nothing to do with the harmonies I had heard before. Then I heard the Claude Thornhill band and all of a sudden my ears started to be intrigued by the more advanced harmony. And I started to play that way on the clarinet. And all of a sudden I was getting criticized, you know, “You’re playing wrong notes.” You know back then it was like forbidden territory. Then all of a sudden the saxophone came into vogue, my first biggest influence in my life on saxophone was Paul Desmond.
Can I wind back just for a second?
